title: Working With Element Collections
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of working with element collections in a jQuery application.
Apply iterating through matched elements in a small example and describe its expected result.
Verify using .each() with an explicit test or browser observation.
status_note: Draft generated from the attached syllabus and official references; requires lesson-by-lesson technical review, local execution, accessibility checks, and editorial approval.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will work through working with element collections with a focused jQuery example. The subtopics below preserve the supplied curriculum coverage and connect the API idea to a small browser interface.
content.why_it_matters: This topic is useful because it turns iterating through matched elements into a repeatable implementation choice. DOM manipulation changes document content. Use text setters for plain text, create elements with known attributes, and avoid inserting untrusted data as HTML.

content_blocks.text: Start with a known DOM structure, apply the pattern for working with element collections, and test one normal case plus one edge case. Keep selectors scoped to the intended component and verify the real browser result.

task_acceptance_criteria: The implementation demonstrates working with element collections using a current, documented approach.
The learner records the expected and actual behavior and checks at least one edge case.
The example preserves semantic HTML and does not render untrusted data as HTML.
The test setup and any runtime limitation are documented honestly.
hints: First identify which DOM nodes and runtime state are involved in working with element collections.
Make one small change, inspect the resulting element or request, and compare it with the expected result.
If the result differs, check the selector, script order, browser console, event target, and relevant API documentation before adding more code.
content.expected_output: Logs the text of every matched .price element.
common_mistakes: Assuming a selector matched an element without checking the collection length.
Confusing jQuery collections with native DOM elements or live properties with markup attributes.
Using .html() with untrusted data or assuming client-side validation enforces server rules.
Treating a demo snippet as production-ready without testing failure and accessibility states.
